Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/

# Cloudy Cloud: Claude Code subagents on their own cloud machines

> Cloudy Cloud is open-source software (MIT license, install with npx cloudycloud setup) that gives every Claude Code subagent its own cloud machine, a copy of your repo, and its own branch.

Every Claude Code subagent gets its own cloud machine, a copy of your repo, and its own branch. Your laptop stays free for you.

## Run it from your laptop. Run it at any scale.

Subagents on your laptop share its CPU, memory and battery with you. Their builds and tests slow your session down. With Cloudy Cloud you still start and steer everything from your laptop, but the work runs on machines in the cloud.

## Every subagent gets its own computer.

When your Claude Code session starts a subagent, Cloudy Cloud gives it a fresh cloud machine. The subagent runs a full Claude Code there, on a copy of your repo. Your laptop only runs your own session.

- Sees your tracked files, including uncommitted edits
- Runs in the cloud, not on your laptop

## Work comes back as a branch.

Each subagent commits and pushes to its own branch on your GitHub repo, named `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Open a pull request from it, or pull it down with one `git fetch`.

- One branch per subagent
- Your local folder stays as you left it

## Keep the conversation going.

A subagent stays open after it answers. Send it another message and it carries on with the same context. It stops on its own after 60 idle minutes, or when your session ends.

- Same context for every follow-up
- Idle machines stop by themselves

## One subagent, or fifty.

Start as many subagents as the task needs. Cloudy Cloud queues them and starts machines as fast as your cloud plan allows. Your plan's machine limit caps how many run at once.

**50** subagents run at once in our tests, on a paid plan

**60 min** idle time before a subagent stops

## Install once, then use subagents as usual.

### Run the installer

1. Run `npx -y cloudycloud setup` in a terminal. It checks your tools and installs the `cloudy-cloud` command and the Cloudy Cloud skills.

### Add your keys

2. Setup asks for your cloud, Claude and GitHub keys and tells you where to get each. Or run `npx skills add dennisonbertram/cloudycloud` and ask Claude to "set up Cloudy Cloud".

### Start a session

3. Run `cloudy-cloud` instead of `claude`, then `git fetch origin cloudy-cloud/<id>` to pull a subagent's work. Plain `claude` is unchanged.

```
$ npx cloudycloud setup
  █▀▀ █   █▀█ █ █ █▀▄ █▄█   █▀▀ █   █▀█ █ █ █▀▄
  █▄▄ █▄▄ █▄█ █▄█ █▄▀  █    █▄▄ █▄▄ █▄█ █▄█ █▄▀
  Checks your tools, links the command and saves your keys.

  ●━━○━━○━━○  Tools  1 of 4
  ✔ git, node, npm, curl and claude are installed
  ✔ Dependencies installed
  ✔ cloudy-cloud already runs from this folder
  ✔ Fleet skill available in every project

  ●━━●━━○━━○  Instabox key  2 of 4
  ? Instabox API key
    Create one at https://dashboard.instabox.sh/dashboard/api-keys
  › Paste it (nothing shows as you paste):
```

```
$ cloudy-cloud
❯ Use three cloud subagents in parallel. Each one adds
  a one-line comment to the top of README.md saying
  hello from agent N, commits, and pushes its branch.
  Then summarise the branch names.
  Called cloud 3 times
⏺ All three agents finished and pushed their branches.
  I fetched each branch and checked it: each one
  changes only README.md.
  ┌───────┬───────────────────────┬─────────┐
  │ Agent │        Branch         │ Commit  │
  ├───────┼───────────────────────┼─────────┤
  │ 1     │ cloudy-cloud/569dac7c │ e4b7bf3 │
  │ 2     │ cloudy-cloud/9b7701a9 │ b6968f1 │
  │ 3     │ cloudy-cloud/5415161c │ 2007b13 │
  └───────┴───────────────────────┴─────────┘
  All three agents ran on Haiku 4.5, and together they
  cost about $0.18.
✻ Cooked for 15s
```

```
$ git fetch origin
$ git branch -r --list "origin/cloudy-cloud/*"
  origin/cloudy-cloud/569dac7c  Add hello from agent 1 comment to README
  origin/cloudy-cloud/9b7701a9  Add hello from agent 2 comment to README
  origin/cloudy-cloud/5415161c  Add hello from agent 3 comment to README
$ git merge origin/cloudy-cloud/569dac7c
```

Real output, lightly trimmed.

## Claude for your session. Your choice of model for workers.

Workers can use Claude, or GLM, DeepSeek, Particle or OpenRouter with your own provider key. Send bulk, well-specified work to a cheaper open model and keep Claude for the hard parts.

Claude — your normal login

GLM — profile: glm

DeepSeek — profile: deepseek

Particle — profile: particle

OpenRouter — profile: openrouter

Your own provider

## Other ways to run agents in the cloud.

Cloud sandboxes give you machines. Hosted agents give you their own agent in their own app. Cloudy Cloud plugs cloud machines into the Claude Code session you already use.

| Product | Starts from your local Claude Code session | One machine per subagent | Results land as | Models for workers | Hosted app, no setup |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cloudy Cloud | Yes | Yes | A git branch per subagent | Claude or open models (GLM, DeepSeek, OpenRouter) | No, you run it yourself |
| Claude Code on the web | No, a separate cloud session | No, subagents share the session's machine | A branch and pull request | Claude only | Yes |
| Cloud sandboxes: Instabox, boat, Maritime, E2B, Daytona | No, you wire it up yourself | You build it | Files on the machine | Whatever you install | Machines and an API, not an agent |
| Hosted coding agents: Codex cloud, Cursor, Copilot, Devin | No, their own agent and app | One machine per task | A branch or pull request | The vendor's choice | Yes |

Based on each product's public docs, November 2026. Products change; check their docs for the latest.

## Questions, answered simply.

### What is a subagent?

When Claude Code hands a piece of work to a helper agent, that helper is a subagent. Cloudy Cloud runs each helper on its own cloud machine instead of on your laptop.

### What do I need?

An account with a cloud sandbox provider (Instabox is supported today), a Claude subscription or API key, a GitHub repo you can push to, and Node.js 20 or later.

### What can a subagent see?

Files tracked by git in your repo, including uncommitted edits. It can't see untracked files or your personal Claude settings. It has MCP servers only if you copy them with `cloudy-cloud mcp add`.

### What happens to the machines?

A subagent stops after 60 idle minutes or when your session ends. Its machine is deleted after 6 hours by default, 24 at most. Only work pushed to GitHub is kept.

### Is it safe?

Your GitHub token never reaches the cloud machine. Subagents run with permission checks off, so protect your main branch. The [setup guide](https://github.com/dennisonbertram/cloudycloud/blob/HEAD/docs/RUNBOOK.md) shows how.

### Does it change plain `claude`?

No. Only sessions you start with `cloudy-cloud` use the cloud.

### Is there a hosted version?

Not yet. A hosted version is coming. Today Cloudy Cloud is open source (MIT) and you bring your own keys: your cloud account, your Claude credentials and your GitHub token.

## Send your subagents up.

`$ npx -y cloudycloud setup` [Read the docs](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/)


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/

# Getting started

> Install Cloudy Cloud, start a session and run your first subagent on a cloud machine.

Cloudy Cloud runs each Claude Code subagent on its own cloud machine, with a copy of your repo and its own branch. You stay in your local Claude Code session and fetch the finished work from GitHub.

## Before you start

You need these accounts and tools:

- **An Instabox account.** Instabox is the cloud provider supported today. The free plan is too small for more than a few subagents at once; swarms need a paid plan.
- **A Claude subscription or an Anthropic API key.** Subagents use a long-lived token from `claude setup-token`. An API key works too but is billed separately.
- **A GitHub repository you can push to.** The repo you work in must have a `github.com` remote named `origin`.
- **On your computer:** macOS or Linux (tested on macOS), `git`, Node.js 20 or later, `npm`, `curl`, and [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com) signed in.

## Install

### Run the installer with npx

```
npx -y cloudycloud setup
```

The `-y` skips npm's own "Ok to proceed?" question. Without it, npm asks that first; answer `y`.

### Or add the skill and ask Claude

```
npx skills add dennisonbertram/cloudycloud
```

Then ask Claude to "set up Cloudy Cloud". Claude checks your tools and asks you to run `npx -y cloudycloud setup` yourself, because setup asks for secret keys that Claude should not see.

### From source

```
git clone https://github.com/dennisonbertram/cloudycloud.git
cd cloudycloud
./install.sh
```

Run it in a terminal. It asks for keys, so it does not work from a pipe. It checks your tools, offers to install `cloudy-cloud` onto your PATH (`npm install -g cloudycloud` for the npx route, `npm link` from source). If an older `cloudy-cloud` command is already installed, setup says so and offers to replace it; if npm still fails, setup prints the fix commands and carries on, and you can use `npx cloudycloud` instead, copies the Cloudy Cloud skills into `~/.claude/skills/`, and then asks for three keys. Cloud coordinators are set up only from source for now. Nothing shows as you paste, and only the last four characters are printed back.

| Key | Where to get it |
|---|---|
| Instabox API key (`ibk_…`) | Create it at [dashboard.instabox.sh](https://dashboard.instabox.sh/dashboard/api-keys). The installer checks it with Instabox before saving. |
| Claude token (`sk-ant-oat01-…`) | Run `claude setup-token` in another terminal, or press Enter at the Claude step and let the installer get it. Your own `claude` login is not changed. |
| GitHub token | Create a [fine-grained token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new) limited to the repos you will use, with Contents set to read and write. The Instabox command-line tool asks for it. |

The Instabox key and Claude token are saved in `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env`. The folder has mode 700 and the file is readable only by your user. The GitHub token is stored in Instabox as the secret `GH_TOKEN`. A subagent's machine only gets a placeholder, never the token.

Later, `cloudy-cloud setup` runs the installer again from any folder. It shows each saved key masked and asks before replacing it. Restart any open session to use new keys.

> Warning: Subagents can push to any branch your GitHub token reaches. Add a branch ruleset that blocks direct pushes to your main branch (GitHub: Settings, Rules, Rulesets).

## Start a session

Run `cloudy-cloud` from inside your repo, instead of `claude`. The package installs the same command under two names, `cloudy-cloud` and `cloudycloud`; use either. If you skipped the global install, run `npx cloudycloud` instead; everything below works the same:

```
cd <your repo>
cloudy-cloud
```

This is an ordinary Claude Code session with one change: the built-in `Agent` tool is turned off, and every subagent goes to a cloud machine through the `cloud_agent` tools. Plain `claude` is unaffected. If a key is missing, `cloudy-cloud` says `cloudy-cloud is not set up yet` and offers to run setup. If the folder is not a git repo, or has no `github.com` origin, it warns you that subagents cannot start or push.

### Run without the interactive UI

Pass a prompt with `-p` to run once and print the answer. Any argument other than the Cloudy Cloud commands goes to Claude Code:

```
cloudy-cloud -p "use a subagent to run hostname, then report the result"
```

Without a terminal there is nobody to approve permission prompts, so your session cannot run commands such as `git fetch` to check a subagent's branch. Allow the commands you want with `--allowedTools`, or pick a mode with `--permission-mode` (`acceptEdits`, `auto`, `bypassPermissions`, `manual`, `dontAsk` or `plan`):

```
cloudy-cloud -p "<prompt>" --allowedTools "Bash(git fetch *)" "Bash(git show *)"
```

Put `--allowedTools` after the prompt, because it takes a list. See `claude --help` for all options. `cloudy-cloud --help` prints Cloudy Cloud's own help, and `cloudy-cloud --version` prints the version.

## Your first subagent

Ask in plain language. This prompt is the runbook's check that everything works:

```
use a subagent to run hostname, write it to proof.txt, commit and push, and tell me the result
```

Claude starts the subagent and returns at once. In a terminal session on Claude Code 2.1.304 or later, the footer shows a count such as `3 MCP tasks`, and `/tasks` lists each subagent with a progress line, for example:

```
12 tool uses · 48.2k tokens · 3m10s · Edit src/parser.ts
```

`starting machine…` means the machine is not up yet. When the subagent finishes, its result reaches Claude automatically. In the VS Code extension, the desktop app, or a one-shot `claude -p` run, Claude calls `cloud_agent_wait` instead.

The answer should name a hostname starting with `instabox-sbx-` and end with `Pushed to origin cloudy-cloud/<id> at <sha>`.

The subagent stays open for follow-up messages until it is stopped. It is stopped after 60 idle minutes, and all subagents are stopped when the session ends.

> Note: Subagents see only files tracked by git, including uncommitted edits to tracked files. They do not see untracked files or your settings. They have MCP servers only if you copy them with `cloudy-cloud mcp add`; see [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).

## Get the work back

Nothing is copied into your local repo automatically. Each subagent pushes to its own branch, `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Fetch it:

```
git fetch origin cloudy-cloud/<id>
git show FETCH_HEAD:proof.txt
```

Then check out, merge, cherry-pick or open a pull request from the branch with ordinary git. For example, `git merge FETCH_HEAD` merges what you just fetched. To fetch every subagent branch at once:

```
git fetch origin 'refs/heads/cloudy-cloud/*:refs/remotes/origin/cloudy-cloud/*'
```

## Stop and clean up

Ask Claude to "stop all subagents", which calls `cloud_agent_stop` and deletes their machines. In `/tasks`, select a task and press `x` to stop a single subagent.

- An idle subagent is stopped after 60 minutes.
- Every subagent is stopped when you exit the session.
- Separately, the Instabox server deletes each worker machine after a fixed time (default 6 hours, set by `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS`, maximum 24).

> Warning: A deleted machine takes unpushed work with it. Only work the subagent pushed to GitHub survives. Fetch what you need before you exit.

To list leftover machines, run `npx instabox@latest ls`. To delete one, run `npx instabox@latest rm <name>`.

## Next steps

- [How it works](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/how-it-works.html): what runs where, and what a subagent can see.
- [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html): run workers on open models.
- [Dashboard and app previews](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/dashboard.html): watch your machines in a local web page.
- [Troubleshooting, security and FAQ](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/troubleshooting.html): fix a missing key, a failed push or a queued subagent.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/how-it-works.html

# How it works

> What runs where when a subagent runs on a cloud machine, what it can see, and how its work comes back.

The `cloudy-cloud` command starts Claude Code with its built-in subagents turned off. Every subagent runs on its own cloud machine and pushes its work to a branch on GitHub.

## One subagent, start to finish

1. **You start `cloudy-cloud` in a git repo.** It launches Claude Code with the built-in `Agent` and `Workflow` tools disabled, an extra system prompt, and an MCP server that provides the `cloud_agent` tools. The system prompt tells Claude to use `cloud_agent` for anything that would have used a subagent.
2. **Claude calls `cloud_agent`** with a prompt and a short description. The call returns at once while the machine starts.
3. **A snapshot of your repo is made.** It holds the committed files plus your uncommitted edits to tracked files. It is made without touching your working tree or index.
4. **A machine is created** from the Instabox `agent-browser` image, and the GitHub token is attached to it as a proxy secret (see Secrets).
5. **The snapshot is uploaded** as a git bundle and checked out on a new branch, `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. The branch is pushed to your `origin` remote right away. If the bundle is over about 9 MB, only the commits GitHub does not already have are uploaded. If that is still too large, the start fails and asks you to push the branch first.
6. **Claude runs on the machine** with `claude -p` in the repo folder. The subagent is told to commit after each meaningful step and to push to its own branch only.
7. **After the turn, the tool pushes once more** in case the subagent forgot (and retries once if GitHub rejects it). It never commits for the subagent. If files were left uncommitted, the reply lists them.
8. **The result comes back** with the branch name and commit, and token and tool-use totals.

Fetch the work with `git fetch origin cloudy-cloud/<id>`. The repo needs a `github.com` origin, because each subagent pushes there.

### Getting the result: task mode or wait

- **Task mode.** When your Claude Code supports MCP tasks, `cloud_agent` becomes a background task. Its progress shows in `/tasks` and the result arrives on its own.
- **Otherwise,** `cloud_agent` returns an `agent_id` and Claude calls `cloud_agent_wait` to collect the result. The default wait is 600 seconds and the maximum is 1500. Each result is marked as reported, so a later wait does not repeat it.

One task is stopped after 29 minutes.

## The five tools

| Tool | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cloud_agent` | Starts a subagent in a new machine. |
| `cloud_agent_message` | Sends a follow-up to an open, idle agent. It continues the same Claude session on the same machine. It is rejected if the agent is busy or gone. |
| `cloud_agent_wait` | Waits for agents to finish their current turn and returns their results. |
| `cloud_agent_list` | Lists every agent with its status, idle minutes and progress (tool uses, tokens, elapsed time, current step). |
| `cloud_agent_stop` | Stops agents and deletes their machines. It is safe to repeat. |

An agent's status is one of `queued`, `starting`, `running`, `idle`, `failed` or `stopped`. After a turn ends, the agent is `idle` and its machine stays open for follow-ups.

## How long a machine lives

| What ends it | When |
|---|---|
| You or Claude call `cloud_agent_stop` | Immediately. |
| Idle timeout | 60 minutes after the agent went idle. |
| Session end | When you quit Claude Code, `cloudy-cloud` deletes every open machine. |
| Cleanup process | A separate process deletes the session's machines after the session is gone, even after a hard kill. It checks every 2 seconds. |
| Delete deadline | Instabox deletes the machine at a fixed time in any state. The default is 6 hours. Set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS` to change it, up to 24. |

> Warning: Only work that a subagent has pushed to GitHub survives if its machine is lost. The deadline cannot be extended, and the subagent is told its deadline so it can push in time.

## Starting many at once

You can start many subagents at once. `cloudy-cloud` paces the starts for Instabox's limits.

- At most 25 machines start per minute, in the order requested. Set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_STARTS_PER_MIN` to change this. A waiting subagent shows the status `queued`, for example `queued for a machine (12 ahead)`.
- If Instabox answers `rate_limited`, the start is retried after the delay Instabox gives, up to 5 tries.
- If your plan's machine limit is full (`quota_exceeded`), the subagent stays queued, retries every 60 seconds for up to 30 minutes, and then fails with Instabox's message.
- At most 24 Instabox command and file requests run at once (`CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_INSTABOX_CALLS`). Working subagents share them in turn.
- One session can start at most 200 agents (`CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_AGENTS_PER_SESSION`).

Your plan's machine limit still caps how many run at the same time. The rest wait in the queue.

## What reaches the machine

- **GitHub token:** not sent to the machine. The machine gets a placeholder named `GH_TOKEN`, and Instabox's proxy swaps in the real token for requests to `github.com` and `api.github.com`.
- **Claude credential:** sent to the machine, as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. For a subagent on another model, the provider key for that profile is sent instead of your Claude credential.
- **MCP server tokens:** only if you added a server that needs one. The token stays in Instabox as a secret named `MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN`, and the machine sees a placeholder that Instabox replaces in request headers to the host you chose. With `mcp add --allow-literal` the real value is on the machine instead.
- **Instabox API key:** not sent to the machine. It stays in your config file and the local server.

> Warning: Each machine runs Claude with permission checks off, and the Claude credential is on it. A prompt injection on the machine could misuse or leak that credential. A subagent can also push to any branch the GitHub token can reach, so protect your main branch.

Output shown to you is scrubbed of known key values. See [Troubleshooting, security and FAQ](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/troubleshooting.html) for more.

## What does not happen

- Nothing is copied into your local repo. Your branch, working tree and index are not changed. You fetch the branch yourself.
- Untracked files are not sent. If a subagent needs a new file, `git add` it first (staging counts as tracked) or commit it.
- Your local MCP servers are not available on the machine, except the ones you copy with `cloudy-cloud mcp add` (remote `https` servers and `npx` or `uvx` servers). See [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).
- Your settings and agents from `~/.claude/agents` are not available on the machine.
- A subagent's own subagents run inside the same machine, not on new ones.

## Why the cloud

Subagents run on remote machines, so your laptop stays free for your own work. You can run many at once, limited by your Instabox plan and the pacing above, instead of by your computer.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html

# Models and keys

> Choose Claude or an open model for a subagent and set up the keys each one needs.

Cloudy Cloud uses your own keys. By default each subagent runs Claude, and you can run a subagent on another model by naming a profile.

## Bring your own keys

Each user supplies their own credentials, because Anthropic's terms require each end user to use their own.

You pay your providers directly. Cloudy Cloud does not resell model access, and this page gives no prices.

## Claude credentials

Subagents need one Claude credential. The setup step (`cloudy-cloud setup`) asks for it. Two kinds work:

- **A token from `claude setup-token`** (starts with `sk-ant-oat01-`). This uses your Claude subscription. At the Claude step, press Enter and setup runs `claude setup-token` for you, or paste a token you made yourself. Setup checks the token with one small Claude request. It is saved as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.
- **An Anthropic API key** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). Setup does not ask for it. Add the line `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...` to the env file yourself (see below). Usage is billed per use.

If both are saved, subagents use the token and not the API key.

Setup saves all keys to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env`. Setup creates the folder with mode 700 and writes the file so that only your user account can read it. The file is plain text with one `NAME=value` line per key. To use another location, set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_CONFIG`.

## Default model and choosing another

With no `profile`, a subagent runs Claude. To pick a Claude model, pass the optional `model` argument of `cloud_agent`, for example `haiku`.

To run a subagent on a non-Claude model, pass the `profile` argument of `cloud_agent`. Do not use `model` for non-Claude models. You can ask in plain language, for example "use a glm subagent for this". Follow-up messages to that subagent reuse its profile.

## Built-in profiles

| Profile | Provider | Model id | Key needed | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code on the model. |
| `deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code on the model. |
| `particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs Claude Code on the model. |
| `pi-glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the pi coding agent, not Claude Code. |
| `pi-deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the pi coding agent. |
| `pi-particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the pi coding agent. |
| `omp-glm` | Particle.ai | `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the oh-my-pi (`omp`) coding agent, not Claude Code. |
| `omp-deepseek` | Particle.ai | `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v41-flash-1017` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the oh-my-pi coding agent. |
| `omp-particle` | Particle.ai | `particle-ai/particle-1` | `PARTICLE_API_KEY` | Runs the oh-my-pi coding agent. |
| `openrouter` | OpenRouter | None built in. You pass one. | `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | See OpenRouter. |

A profile worker receives only its own provider key. It never receives your Claude credential. If the key for a profile is missing, `cloud_agent` fails at once and names the key.

### The pi profiles

The `pi-*` profiles run the [pi coding agent](https://pi.dev) in the worker instead of Claude Code. They use none of your Claude allowance. A pi profile is for workers only, because coordinators always run Claude Code. Results from pi workers have no cost line. They get the MCP servers from `cloudy-cloud mcp add`, except `sse` servers, because pi has no SSE transport. See [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).

### The omp profiles

The `omp-*` profiles run [oh-my-pi](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi) (the `omp` command) in the worker instead of Claude Code. oh-my-pi is a fork of pi rewritten as a coding-first agent. It adds LSP support, persistent Python and Bun kernels, subagents and many providers. The profiles use the same three Particle.ai models as the pi profiles, and none of your Claude allowance.

Each omp worker installs the pinned oh-my-pi release v18.18.7 with the official installer, which checks the binary's SHA-256. The binary is about 243 MB and is downloaded on every omp worker, so an omp worker starts slower than a pi or Claude worker. In one live check the whole omp worker setup (clone, first push, omp install and config) took about 20 seconds from machine creation to running, against 11 seconds for a pi worker started at the same time (one run each). An omp profile is for workers only, because coordinators always run Claude Code. Results from omp workers have no cost line. A follow-up resumes the same omp session. omp workers get the servers from `cloudy-cloud mcp add`, including `sse` servers.

## OpenRouter

To use OpenRouter:

1. Create a key at [openrouter.ai/keys](https://openrouter.ai/keys).
2. Run `cloudy-cloud setup` and paste it at the OpenRouter step. It is saved as `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.
3. Start a subagent with `profile: "openrouter"` and pass the OpenRouter model id in `model`. This is the one case where `model` goes with a non-Claude model, because the profile has no built-in model.

If you pass no model, the call fails with "needs a model". To avoid passing it every time, set a `model` for `openrouter` in `profiles.json` (below).

> Note: Signing in with OpenRouter or ChatGPT is not available. You paste an API key.

## Your own profiles

Create `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/profiles.json` (or point `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROFILES` at another file) to override a built-in profile or add one:

```
{
  "openrouter": {
    "format": "anthropic",
    "baseUrl": "https://openrouter.ai/api",
    "model": "MODEL-ID",
    "keyName": "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
  }
}
```

`format` is `anthropic` or `openai`. `keyName` must be a key in your env file whose name ends in `_API_KEY`. An optional `"harness"` is `"claude"` (the default), `"pi"` or `"omp"`. `"pi"` runs the pi agent and `"omp"` runs oh-my-pi. Replace `MODEL-ID` with a model id from your provider.

## Adding or changing keys later

- Run `cloudy-cloud setup` again. It shows each saved key masked and asks before replacing it. The Particle.ai and OpenRouter steps are optional: press Enter to skip.
- Or edit `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` directly. Keep the file private. To remove all saved keys, delete it.
- Restart `cloudy-cloud` afterwards. It reads keys once at start, so a running session keeps the old ones.

> Warning: A provider key is stored on each worker machine that uses that profile. A prompt-injected worker could read it. Use keys you can revoke.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/reference.html

# Command and tool reference

> Every cloudy-cloud command, MCP tool, option and environment variable.

This page lists every `cloudy-cloud` command and flag, the five tools Claude uses to run cloud agents, and the environment variables and files that change how they behave.

## Command line

These commands run on your computer. `cloudy-cloud` checks the first argument. If it is `dashboard`, `open`, `coordinator`, `setup` or `--setup`, it runs that command. `mcp ls`, `mcp add NAME`, `mcp add NAME --allow-literal` and `mcp rm NAME` run cloudy-cloud mcp; any other `mcp` arguments go to Claude Code. Any other arguments start a Claude Code session.

### cloudy-cloud

```
cloudy-cloud [claude arguments]
```

The package installs the same command under two names, `cloudy-cloud` and `cloudycloud`; use either. Without a global install, `npx cloudycloud` runs the same command. Plain `claude` is not affected.

Starts a normal Claude Code session in the current folder. In that session the built-in `Agent` and `Workflow` tools are denied, and Claude starts subagents with the five cloud tools described below. Run it from inside a git repository that has a `github.com` origin, because each cloud agent pushes its work to a branch there.

Every argument is passed to `claude` after the flags that `cloudy-cloud` adds itself (`--mcp-config`, `--settings` and `--append-system-prompt`). There are no `cloudy-cloud` flags of its own for a session.

Before it starts Claude, the command checks three things:

- It needs an Instabox API key (from the environment or the config file) and a Claude token or Anthropic API key in the config file. If one is missing, it tells you. In a terminal it offers to run `cloudy-cloud setup` now. Outside a terminal it exits with status 1.
- If the folder is not a git repository, it prints a warning that subagents cannot start.
- If the repository has no `github.com` origin, it prints a warning that subagents cannot push their work.

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud --model opus
```

It also sets `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` to 1800000 (30 minutes) unless you already set it.

### cloudy-cloud --help and --version

```
cloudy-cloud --help
cloudy-cloud --version
```

`--help` (also `-h` or `help`, when it is the only argument) prints Cloudy Cloud's own commands, then points to `claude --help` for Claude Code's options. `--version` prints the Cloudy Cloud version. With any other arguments, everything goes to Claude Code, for example `cloudy-cloud -p "<prompt>" --allowedTools "Bash(git fetch *)"`; see [Run without the interactive UI](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/#no-interactive-ui).

### cloudy-cloud setup

```
cloudy-cloud setup [--check-only]
```

Runs the bundled `install.sh`, whatever folder you are in. `cloudy-cloud --setup` does the same, and `npx -y cloudycloud setup` runs it without installing anything first (`-y` skips npm's "Ok to proceed?" question). Setup checks your tools, offers to install the `cloudy-cloud` command (`npm install -g cloudycloud`, or a link when you run it from a git clone), copies the Cloudy Cloud skills into `~/.claude/skills`, and asks for your Instabox key, your Claude token and your GitHub token, then offers optional steps for model provider keys and cloud coordinators. If an older `cloudy-cloud` global command blocks the install, setup offers to replace it (`npm rm -g cloudy-cloud`, then `npm install -g cloudycloud`). Run it again to change a key. It needs a terminal because it asks for keys. See [Getting started](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--check-only` | Check that `git`, Node.js, `npm`, `curl` and `claude` are installed, then exit. Does not need a terminal and changes nothing. |

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud setup --check-only
```

### cloudy-cloud dashboard

```
cloudy-cloud dashboard [--demo] [--port N] [--no-open]
```

Starts a read-only web page on `127.0.0.1` that shows your cloud agents, coordinators and the messages between your session and them. It prints a link that contains a random token for this run, and opens it in your browser. Press Ctrl+C to stop it. There is no `--help` option. See [Dashboard and app previews](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/dashboard.html).

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--demo` | Show sample data instead of your machines. Nothing in it is real. |
| `--port N` | Listen on port N, from 0 to 65535. The default is 4477. If that port is in use, the dashboard uses a free port instead. Port 0 always picks a free port. |
| `--no-open` | Only print the link. Do not open a browser. |

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud dashboard --port 5000 --no-open
```

### cloudy-cloud open

```
cloudy-cloud open <agent-id-or-machine> <port> [--share]
cloudy-cloud open <agent-id-or-machine> <port> --unshare
```

Reaches an app, such as a dev server, that runs on a cloud agent's machine. The first argument is an agent id (the `<id>` in the branch `cloudy-cloud/<id>`, shown by `cloud_agent_list`), a machine name or a machine id (a coordinator's machine is named `coord-NAME`). It may use only letters, digits, dots, dashes and underscores. The machine must be running. The command needs your Instabox key.

With no flag, it opens a private tunnel from `http://127.0.0.1:<port>` on your computer to that port on the machine. It runs until you press Ctrl-C. Start the app in the background on the machine (for example `nohup npm run dev > /tmp/dev.log 2>&1 &`), because the foreground processes of a turn end with the turn. The tunnel and any shared link stop when the machine is deleted.

| Argument or flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<port>` | A port from 1 to 65535 on the machine. Write `LOCAL:REMOTE` to use a different port on your computer (not allowed with `--share` or `--unshare`). |
| `--share` | Publish a private link, with a token in the URL, instead of a tunnel. Anyone who has the link can open the app until the machine is deleted or you unshare it. It never publishes publicly. |
| `--unshare` | Remove the link for that port. Cannot be combined with `--share`. |

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud open 3f9a1c2e 5173
```

### cloudy-cloud coordinator

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator image [--save]
cloudy-cloud coordinator start NAME --repo URL [--branch B] [--task TEXT | --task-file PATH] [--max-hours N] [--json]
cloudy-cloud coordinator attach NAME
cloudy-cloud coordinator ls
cloudy-cloud coordinator stop NAME
cloudy-cloud coordinator finish [--force]
```

Manages cloud coordinators: long-lived Claude Code sessions that run on their own Instabox machines and start workers there. All subcommands except `finish` need your Instabox key. With any other first argument, or none, the command prints this usage line. See [Coordinators and fleets](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/fleets.html) for when to use them.

#### coordinator image

Builds the machine image that coordinators start from. It is a one-time step. Without `--save`, it creates an image machine, installs cloudy-cloud on it, and prints the steps to sign in to Claude on it (`claude auth login` in a shell on the machine). With `--save`, it saves a snapshot of that machine, stores its id as `CLOUDY_CLOUD_COORDINATOR_SNAPSHOT` in the config file, and deletes the image machine. The server deletes an unsaved image machine after 2 hours. Only one image machine can exist at a time.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--save` | Save the signed-in image machine as a snapshot and delete the machine. |

#### coordinator start

Starts a coordinator named NAME on a new machine from the saved image. It sends the current checkout of cloudy-cloud, writes the coordinator's key file (mode 600), clones your repository to `~/repo`, and starts Claude Code in a `tmux` session called `claude`, with Remote Control under the name NAME. The coordinator never pauses. The server deletes its machine after `--max-hours`. You can reach it from claude.ai/code or the Claude app (pick the session named NAME) or from a terminal with `coordinator attach`. The first time, attach once and accept any trust or Remote Control prompts.

| Argument or flag | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `NAME` | required | Lowercase letters, digits and `-`, up to 40 characters, starting with a letter or digit. A coordinator with the same name must not already exist. |
| `--repo URL` | required | A `https://github.com/OWNER/REPO` URL. |
| `--branch B` | the repository's default branch | Branch to clone. |
| `--task TEXT` | none | A task for the coordinator to start on. Up to 100,000 bytes. Cannot be empty. |
| `--task-file PATH` | none | Read the task from a local file instead. Same limits. |
| `--max-hours N` | 24 | Hours until the server deletes the machine. At most 24, at least 60 seconds (1/60 hour). The deadline cannot be extended. |
| `--json` | off | Print one line of JSON with `name`, `machine`, `remoteControlName` and `attach` instead of the usual text. |

If neither `--task` nor `--task-file` is given, the coordinator starts without a task. The command fails with a message if no coordinator image has been saved.

Example:

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator start docs-fleet --repo https://github.com/OWNER/REPO --task-file task.md --max-hours 8
```

#### coordinator attach

Prints the command that opens the coordinator's `tmux` session over SSH. It does not run the command. Copy it into your terminal. It has the form `npx --yes instabox@latest ssh <machine> -- tmux attach -t claude`.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator attach docs-fleet
```

#### coordinator ls

Lists your coordinators in a table with the columns NAME, STATE, STARTED (CREATED when the output is not a terminal), MACHINE and DELETES. It prints `No coordinators.` when there are none.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator ls
```

#### coordinator stop

Deletes the coordinator's machine now. Its workers are deleted by the coordinator's cleanup process, or at their own deadline (6 hours by default). Anything the coordinator did not push to GitHub is lost.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator stop docs-fleet
```

#### coordinator finish

Runs on the coordinator machine, started by the coordinator itself when its work is done. It checks that the working tree in `~/repo` is clean, that the current branch and every `fleet/*` branch are pushed to their upstream, and that none of the coordinator's workers are still running. If all checks pass, it deletes its own machine. If a check fails, it lists the problems and deletes nothing. It refuses to run on a machine that is not a coordinator.

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--force` | Skip the git and worker checks and delete the machine anyway. |

> Warning: `--force` can delete work that has not been pushed. Use it only when you accept losing that work.

### cloudy-cloud mcp

```
cloudy-cloud mcp add NAME [--allow-literal]
cloudy-cloud mcp ls
cloudy-cloud mcp rm NAME
```

Chooses which of your Claude Code MCP servers cloud subagents get. `add` copies one server from your Claude Code settings (local, project or user scope) to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json`, replaces a secret value with `${MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN}` and prints the `npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set ... --host ...` command that stores the value once in Instabox. `ls` lists the saved servers and the secrets they need. `rm` removes one. Only `https` servers on public hosts and `npx` or `uvx` servers are accepted; a refused server prints `Not added: REASON` and exits with status 1. `--allow-literal` asks you to confirm and then copies the real token to the machines instead of using an Instabox secret. All of this is described in [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).

## Tools Claude uses (MCP)

`cloudy-cloud` adds an MCP server named `cloud` to the session. Claude sees its tools as `mcp__cloud__cloud_agent` and so on. The session is configured to allow these five tools without asking and to deny the built-in `Agent` and `Workflow` tools. You normally ask for subagents in plain language and Claude calls the tools. This section is for when you want to know exactly what each tool takes.

In a terminal Claude Code session that supports MCP tasks, `cloud_agent` and `cloud_agent_message` run as background tasks. Their progress shows in `/tasks` and the result arrives on its own with the agent id, so Claude does not need `cloud_agent_wait`. In other clients these two tools return an agent id at once and Claude calls `cloud_agent_wait`. The server also answers the task methods `tasks/get` and `tasks/cancel`.

### cloud_agent

Starts a Claude subagent in a remote sandbox on the committed and tracked files of the current repository. It does not include untracked files. The repository needs a `github.com` origin. The call returns at once while the sandbox starts and the task runs. The agent pushes its work to the origin branch `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Nothing is copied into your local repository. The agent stays open for follow-ups until it is stopped or has been idle for 60 minutes.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `prompt` | string | yes | none | The full task for the subagent. |
| `description` | string | yes | none | A short label for the task. |
| `model` | string | no | the Claude default | A Claude model name, such as `haiku`. For a non-Claude model, use `profile` instead. It may contain only letters, digits and `. _ : -`. When `profile` is also set, `/` is allowed too. |
| `profile` | string | no | Claude | Runs the worker on another model. Built in: `glm`, `deepseek`, `particle`, `pi-glm`, `pi-deepseek`, `pi-particle`, `omp-glm`, `omp-deepseek`, `omp-particle` and `openrouter`. You can add names in `profiles.json`. An unknown name, or a profile whose key is missing, makes the call fail at once. See [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html). |
| `role` | string, `worker` or `coordinator` | no | `worker` | A worker does the task. A coordinator also gets cloudy-cloud installed and can start its own cloud agents, limited by `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_DEPTH` (default 3). A coordinator cannot use a `pi-` profile. |
| `subagent_type` | string | no | none | The name of an agent to run, passed to Claude Code as `--agent`. It may contain only letters, digits and `. _ : -`. |

When `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json` holds at least one valid server, a Claude subagent (not a `pi` profile) starts with `--mcp-config` for that file and `--strict-mcp-config`, so a repo's own `.mcp.json` is not loaded on the machine. The reply ends with an `MCP servers:` line. See [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html).

The call is refused if the session has already started `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_AGENTS_PER_SESSION` agents (default 200), or if the folder is not a git repository with at least one commit and a `github.com` origin.

### cloud_agent_message

Sends a follow-up message to an open agent that is idle, and continues the same conversation. It returns at once. As an MCP task the reply arrives on its own. Otherwise Claude calls `cloud_agent_wait`. It is rejected if the agent is busy or gone.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `agent_id` | string | yes | none | The id returned by `cloud_agent`. |
| `message` | string | yes | none | The follow-up text. |

### cloud_agent_wait

Waits until every listed agent finishes its current turn, or until the timeout passes. For each agent it returns the status (`starting`, `running`, `idle`, `failed` or `stopped`) and its latest result. Each result is returned once. Later calls mark it as already reported. The tool is read-only.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `agent_ids` | array of strings | yes | none | The agent ids to wait for. |
| `timeout_seconds` | number | no | 600 | How long to wait. Values above 1500 are limited to 1500. |

### cloud_agent_list

Lists every agent with its id, description, status, idle minutes and progress (tool uses, tokens, elapsed time and current step). The tool is read-only and takes no parameters.

### cloud_agent_stop

Stops agents and deletes their sandboxes. It is safe to repeat, and safe to call with ids that do not exist. Stop agents when they are finished, because they stay open until stopped or idle for 60 minutes.

| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `agent_ids` | array of strings | yes | none | The agent ids to stop. |

### Limits that apply to the tools

- An agent that is idle for 60 minutes is stopped. Every agent is stopped when the session ends.
- A single task is stopped after 29 minutes.
- Machines start at most `CLOUDY_CLOUD_STARTS_PER_MIN` times a minute. Agents waiting for a machine show the status `queued`.
- Instabox deletes every machine the tool creates after `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS` hours, even if `cloudy-cloud` has died.

## Environment variables and files

Environment variables win over values in the config file. An empty value counts as unset.

### Keys

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `INSTABOX_API_KEY` | none | Your Instabox API key. Read from the environment or the config file. |
| `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` | none | The long-lived token from `claude setup-token`. Cloud agents use it to sign in to Claude. |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | none | An Anthropic API key, used by cloud agents when there is no Claude token. It is billed separately. |
| `PARTICLE_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, and any other name ending in `_API_KEY` | none | Provider keys for model profiles. A profile's `keyName` must name one of these. A worker that uses a profile receives that profile's key. |

> Note: The launcher only checks the config file for the Claude token, not the environment, so save it there with `cloudy-cloud setup`. The Instabox key can come from either place.

### Settings

| Variable | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_CONFIG` | `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` | Path of the config file. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROVIDER` | `instabox` | Sandbox provider. Instabox is the only supported value today. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_PROFILES` | `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/profiles.json` | Path of the file that adds or overrides model profiles. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MCP` | `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json` | Path of the file that lists the MCP servers cloud subagents get. If the file is missing, no servers are sent. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_EVENTS` | `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/events.jsonl` | Path of the event log that the dashboard reads. Set it in the environment before you start `cloudy-cloud` and the dashboard. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS` | 6 | Hours until the server deletes a worker or nested coordinator machine. At most 24. A value that is not a positive number uses 6. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_STARTS_PER_MIN` | 25 | The most machine starts per minute. Extra agents wait in the queue. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_INSTABOX_CALLS` | 24 | The most Instabox command and file requests that run at once. Instabox's own limit is 32. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_DEPTH` | 3 | How many levels of coordinators can exist below your session. Starting a coordinator past this is refused. Workers do not add depth. Passed down to child coordinators. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_AGENTS_PER_SESSION` | 200 | How many agents one cloudy-cloud session may start. Passed down to child coordinators. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_CHECK_SECONDS` | 60 | Setup only: how long to wait for the test request that checks your Claude token. |
| `CLOUDY_CLOUD_NO_ANIMATION` | unset | Setup only: set to `1` to skip the animated banner. The banner is also skipped when `CI` is set or there is no terminal. |
| `MCP_TOOL_TIMEOUT` | 1800000 | Claude Code's timeout for one MCP tool call, in milliseconds. The launcher sets it only if you have not. |
| `NO_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR=0`, `TERM=dumb` | unset | Any of these turns off colour and the animated setup display. Output is plain text with the same messages. |

> Note: You can set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_STARTS_PER_MIN`, `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_INSTABOX_CALLS`, `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS`, `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_DEPTH` and `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_AGENTS_PER_SESSION` in the config file as well as in the environment.

### Files

| Path | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` | The config file. One `NAME=value` per line, mode 600. `cloudy-cloud setup` writes it. Only the settings and keys listed above are read from it, plus `CLOUDY_CLOUD_COORDINATOR_SNAPSHOT`, which `coordinator image --save` writes. Change the location with `CLOUDY_CLOUD_CONFIG`. |
| `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/profiles.json` | Optional. Adds or overrides model profiles. See [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html). |
| `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json` | Optional. The MCP servers that cloud subagents get, in Claude Code's `mcpServers` format, mode 600. `cloudy-cloud mcp add` writes it. Secret values are stored as `${MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN}` references unless you used `--allow-literal`. See [MCP servers for subagents](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html). |
| `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/events.jsonl` | The event log. The MCP server appends one JSON line per agent event (agent, message, machine, status, progress, reply). The file has mode 600 inside a folder with mode 700. It holds your prompts and replies, so it stays on your computer. Key-shaped text is redacted before writing, and each text is cut at 20,000 characters. It is never rotated: delete it to clear the history. The dashboard reads the newest 16 MB. |
| `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/owner` | An id the MCP server writes next to the config file, so `coordinator finish` can tell which running machines are its workers. You do not need to edit it. |

If you used the tool under its old name, claude-cloud, the first run copies `~/.config/claude-cloud` to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud` and renames the `CLAUDE_CLOUD_` keys in the config file. The old folder is left in place.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/fleets.html

# Coordinators and fleets

> Run a cloud coordinator that manages many workers, and the limits that apply.

A coordinator is a Claude session that starts and manages many worker agents, each on its own cloud machine. This page covers when to use one, how to run one, and how to merge many worker branches into one pull request.

## When to use a coordinator

For a few independent tasks, start plain cloud agents from your own session. You wait for them and review their branches yourself.

Use a **cloud coordinator** when all of these are true:

- The job is long or large.
- You want to leave, or close your laptop.
- The work needs only what is already on GitHub.

Do not hand a job to a cloud coordinator if it needs untracked local files, secrets or services that exist only on your laptop, or if you want to steer it step by step. Run the fleet from your own session instead.

There is also a lighter option. A cloud agent started with `role: "coordinator"` is a Claude subagent that can start its own cloud agents. Use this to build a tree: a coordinator, sub-coordinators for separate areas of the code, then workers. It lives only as long as your session. A cloud coordinator (below) runs on its own machine and keeps working with your laptop closed.

## Cloud coordinator lifecycle

### 1. Make the coordinator image (once)

Remote Control needs a full Claude login. A token from `claude setup-token` cannot open Remote Control sessions. So you sign in once on an image machine and save it as an Instabox snapshot.

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator image
```

This creates a machine, installs `cloudy-cloud` on it, and prints an SSH command. Run that command, then run this in the shell it opens:

```
claude auth login
```

Finish the browser sign-in, leave the shell, then save the snapshot:

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator image --save
```

This saves the snapshot id as `CLOUDY_CLOUD_COORDINATOR_SNAPSHOT` in `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` and deletes the image machine. The image machine is deleted by the server after 2 hours if you do not finish.

### 2. Start a coordinator

```
cloudy-cloud coordinator start NAME --repo https://github.com/OWNER/REPO --branch main --task-file brief.md
```

- `NAME`: lowercase letters, digits and `-`, up to 40 characters.
- `--repo`: a github.com https URL. The coordinator clones it into `~/repo`.
- `--branch B`: the branch to clone. Optional.
- `--task TEXT` or `--task-file PATH`: the brief. Optional, up to 100 KB. Without one, the coordinator waits for you.
- `--max-hours N`: when the server deletes the machine. Default and maximum 24.
- `--json`: print the machine name, Remote Control name and attach command as JSON.

The coordinator sees only the brief and the repo on GitHub. Commit and push everything it needs first. Give it exact acceptance commands, the files each work package owns, and a default for every question you can foresee, because nobody is there to answer.

### 3. Reach it

- **Remote Control:** open claude.ai/code or the Claude app and pick the session named `NAME`.
- **Terminal:** `cloudy-cloud coordinator attach NAME` prints an SSH command that attaches to its tmux session. Run the command it prints.

The first time, attach once and accept any trust or Remote Control prompts. To list your coordinators and their delete times, run `cloudy-cloud coordinator ls`.

### 4. Finish or stop

- The coordinator ends its own job with `~/cloudy-cloud/bin/cloudy-cloud coordinator finish`. This deletes its machine only if the working tree is clean, the current branch and every `fleet/*` branch are pushed, and no worker is still running. If a check fails it tells you what to fix. `--force` skips the git and worker checks.
- You can delete it at any time with `cloudy-cloud coordinator stop NAME`.
- If neither happens, the server deletes the machine at its deadline.

> Warning: A coordinator is billed until it is stopped, finished or deleted. Its `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env` holds your real Instabox key, your Claude setup-token and your provider API keys, because it needs them to start workers. Anyone who can SSH into the machine can read them. Use keys you can revoke.

## Getting one result from many workers

Each worker pushes a branch named `cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Starting 100 workers is easy. Reviewing 100 pull requests is not. The `cloud-fleet` skill teaches Claude these patterns:

| Situation | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Many unrelated small fixes, and reviewers want separate PRs | Flat fan-out: one PR per branch. Keep it to about 10 to 15. |
| One feature or one large job split across many workers | Trunk merging (the default) |
| Stage B needs the merged result of stage A | Waves |
| More than about 50 workers, or clearly separate areas | Trunk merging with sub-coordinators |

### Trunk merging

The coordinator creates an integration branch `fleet/<topic>` and is the only one that merges into it.

Create and push the trunk before starting workers. Workers copy only tracked files, so commit everything they need first.

```
git fetch origin
git checkout -b fleet/<topic> origin/<base>
git push -u origin fleet/<topic>
```

2. Start the workers. Give each a brief with its goal, the files it owns, the base branch `fleet/<topic>`, the exact test command, and an instruction to push to its `cloudy-cloud/<id>` branch before it finishes.

As workers finish, fetch their branches and merge them one at a time, running the tests after each merge:

```
git fetch origin 'refs/heads/cloudy-cloud/*:refs/remotes/origin/cloudy-cloud/*'
git checkout fleet/<topic>
git merge --no-ff origin/cloudy-cloud/<id> -m "Merge <description> (<id>)"
git push origin fleet/<topic>
```

4. On a conflict, resolve small ones yourself, or abort the merge and ask the worker to rebase. If the tests fail after a merge, do not push it. Send the worker the failing output.
5. When every good branch is merged and the full tests pass, open one PR from `fleet/<topic>`.
6. Delete merged worker branches: `git push origin --delete cloudy-cloud/<id>`. Keep the branch of a failed worker until you decide what to keep.

> Note: Do not trust a worker that says it is done. Fetch its branch, read the diff and run the tests before merging. If a worker pushed nothing, retry it with a narrower brief that names what is missing.

Only push to `cloudy-cloud/*` and `fleet/*` branches. Never push to `main`. Protect your main branch with a GitHub ruleset, because workers run with permission checks off.

### Sub-coordinators and waves

For large jobs, the top coordinator gives each area to a sub-coordinator with its own sub-trunk `fleet/<topic>/<area>`. Each sub-coordinator merges its workers, tests its area, and reports. The top coordinator merges the sub-trunks and opens the PR. Git cannot hold both `fleet/x` and `fleet/x/y`, so if that happens name them `fleet/<topic>-<area>`.

For waves, merge wave 1 into the trunk and push it before you start wave 2. Never start a dependent worker before its dependency is merged and pushed.

Keep coordinators on Claude, because merging and judging results needs a strong model. Open-model workers suit bulk, well-specified tasks. See [Models and keys](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/models.html). Check their branches more carefully.

## Limits and costs to watch

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Cloud coordinator delete deadline | 24 hours by default and at most; set shorter with `--max-hours N`. It cannot be extended. A job that must run longer needs a new coordinator from a pushed branch. |
| Worker and nested coordinator delete deadline | `CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS`, default 6, at most 24 |
| Idle agent | Stopped after 60 minutes with nothing to do |
| One task | Stopped after 29 minutes |
| Nesting depth | `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_DEPTH`, default 3 |
| Agents per session | `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_AGENTS_PER_SESSION`, default 200 |
| Start rate | `CLOUDY_CLOUD_STARTS_PER_MIN`, default 25 a minute. Extra agents show as `queued`. |
| Instabox calls at once | `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MAX_INSTABOX_CALLS`, default 24 |

Every machine in a tree counts against your Instabox machine limit and start rate. If many agents stay `queued`, the machine limit is full. Wait, or use fewer, larger tasks. Stop agents you no longer need with `cloud_agent_stop`, because idle agents cost money until they time out.

> Warning: Only work pushed to GitHub survives. A worker's unpushed work is lost with its machine. When you stop a coordinator, its workers are deleted by its cleanup process or at their own deadline (6 hours by default), so stop or collect them first. Machines your laptop session started are deleted when that session ends, so push or collect their work before you exit.

To see what is running, use the [dashboard](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/dashboard.html).


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/dashboard.html

# Dashboard and app previews

> Watch your cloud agents in a local web page and open apps running on their machines.

The dashboard is a read-only web page on your own computer that shows your cloud agents and the messages between them and your session. To look at an app a cloud agent is running, use `cloudy-cloud open`.

## Start the dashboard

```
cloudy-cloud dashboard
```

This prints a link and opens it in your browser. The page is served from `127.0.0.1` on port 4477, or on a free port if 4477 is taken. Press Ctrl+C in the terminal to stop it.

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--demo` | Shows sample data, so you can look around before you have started any agents. |
| `--port N` | Uses port N (0 to 65535). |
| `--no-open` | Prints the link without opening a browser. |

## What it shows

The page has two views, switched at the top: **List** and **Fleet**.

- **List** has the boxes in a left column and the selected box in a detail pane.
- **Fleet** shows one tile per box, with its status, description, id and time since last activity. Select a tile to open it in the List view.

Boxes are grouped as **Needs you**, **Active** and **Finished**.

- **Needs you:** agents that are idle, and agents that failed today.
- **Active:** agents that are queued, starting or running.
- **Finished:** everything else.

The top bar counts running, starting, idle and failed agents and those finished today. The browser tab title shows the failed and idle counts.

### The detail pane

Select a box to see:

- **Status**, **Model** (or profile) and **Started**.
- **MCP**: the names of the MCP servers the subagent has, when it has any.
- **Branch**: the `cloudy-cloud/<id>` branch, with the result of the last push (the commit hash, or "push failed"), and copy buttons.
- **Deletes**: when the machine is expected to be deleted, for an agent that is still active or idle. For an idle agent this is 60 minutes after it went idle. For an active agent the dashboard shows 8 hours after it started. That is only an upper estimate: the server deletes a worker machine at its own deadline, 6 hours after it starts by default (`CLOUDY_CLOUD_WORKER_HOURS`, at most 24), which can be earlier.
- **Open app**: for a running or idle agent, the command `cloudy-cloud open <id> <port>` with a copy button. See below.
- **Activity**: a timeline of the task you sent, follow-up messages, progress steps, and the agent's replies.

### When something is wrong

- **Offline:** the page cannot reach the dashboard server. It keeps the last list, shows the time of the last update, and retries every 3 seconds. If it has no list yet, it shows *The dashboard cannot reach its server*. Start the server again with `cloudy-cloud dashboard` and open the new link.
- **Old link:** each run makes a new link. A link from an earlier run is refused: a page that is already open shows *This link is from an earlier run*, and a request without the right token gets the text *This dashboard link is missing its access key, or it is from an earlier run.* Open the newest link in your terminal, or run `cloudy-cloud dashboard` again.
- **Live machines unavailable:** a banner appears if the Instabox machine list cannot be read, for example when `INSTABOX_API_KEY` is missing or invalid. Session history still shows.
- **No boxes yet:** an empty list means you have not started an agent from a `cloudy-cloud` session.

## What it cannot show

- **Sessions started before the event log existed.** Their agents have no history. If the machine is still running, it appears as a bare machine with no messages.
- **A cloud coordinator's messages.** A cloud coordinator runs on its own machine, so its messages are not recorded on your computer. It appears as a machine, and its workers appear as machines without a session log. Nested coordinators log on their own machine too.
- **Queued agents.** A queued agent is shown as *starting*.
- **Ended sessions.** An agent from a session that has since ended is shown as stopped.

## Security model

- **Local only.** The server listens on `127.0.0.1`. It answers only requests whose `Host` is `localhost` or `127.0.0.1`.
- **Per-run token.** Each run makes a random token that is part of the link. A request without it gets a 401.
- **Read-only.** It accepts only GET and HEAD requests. It cannot start, message or stop an agent.
- **Keys stay out of the browser.** The Instabox key is used only by the server. Error text is redacted before it is sent to the page.
- **The event log is private to you.** The log is `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/events.jsonl` (set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_EVENTS` to move it), in a folder with mode 700, with file mode 600. Exact secret values are removed, and key-shaped text such as `sk-…`, `ghp_…`, `NAME_KEY=…` and bearer tokens is redacted, before anything is written. Each text is cut at 20,000 characters.

> Note: Prompts and replies can contain your code, and redaction only catches key-shaped text. Treat the log as private. It is never rotated; delete the file to clear the history. The dashboard reads the newest 16 MB of it.

## Reach an app running on an agent's machine

If an agent starts a dev server or a web app, you can view it from your own browser. The dashboard shows the command for each running agent in its **Open app** row. Replace `<port>` with the port the app uses.

### Private tunnel

```
cloudy-cloud open AGENT_ID 3000
```

This forwards `http://127.0.0.1:3000` on your computer to port 3000 on the agent's machine, until you press Ctrl-C. Use an agent id from `cloud_agent_list` (the `<id>` in branch `cloudy-cloud/<id>`), a machine name or a machine id. A coordinator's machine is named `coord-NAME`. To use a different local port, write `LOCAL:REMOTE`, for example `8080:3000`. Only you can reach the tunnel.

### Share a private link

```
cloudy-cloud open AGENT_ID 3000 --share
```

This prints a private link with a token in the URL. It never publishes the app publicly.

> Warning: Anyone who has the link can open the app, until the machine is deleted or you remove the link. Share it only with people who should see the app, and do not paste it where others can read it.

Remove the link with:

```
cloudy-cloud open AGENT_ID 3000 --unshare
```

`--share` and `--unshare` take a single port, not `LOCAL:REMOTE`.

### Two limits

**Start the app in the background.** A turn's foreground processes end with the turn. Ask the agent to run the app like this:

```
nohup npm run dev > /tmp/dev.log 2>&1 &
```

2. **The tunnel and link stop when the machine is deleted.** A worker machine is deleted after 60 idle minutes, when the session ends, or at its deadline (6 hours by default). A coordinator lives longer (24 hours by default).

The command uses the Instabox CLI (`npx --yes instabox@latest`), so you must be signed in to Instabox. If it says you are not, run `cloudy-cloud setup`. If the agent's machine is not running, the command says so and you need to start a new agent.

For running many agents, see [Coordinators and fleets](https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/fleets.html).


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/mcp.html

# MCP servers for subagents

> Choose which of your MCP servers cloud subagents get with cloudy-cloud mcp add, what is allowed, and how tokens stay in Instabox.

Cloud subagents have no MCP servers unless you choose some. `cloudy-cloud mcp add` copies a server from your Claude Code settings to the list that every cloud subagent gets. It is off until you add one.

## Add a server

Three steps. Replace `notion` with the name Claude Code shows in `claude mcp list`.

1. Copy the server: `cloudy-cloud mcp add notion`. It finds the server in your Claude Code settings, shows what it found, and saves it.
2. If the server needs a token, run the `secrets set` command that step 1 printed. You run it once per token.
3. Start subagents as usual. The reply ends with a line such as `MCP servers: notion`.

This is the output for a server that sends a token in a header:

```
cloudy-cloud mcp add notion
Found notion in ~/.claude.json (user scope):
  type     http
  url      https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
  headers  Authorization: Bearer ntn_…9f3a
This server sends a secret. Cloud machines run Claude with permission checks off, so the value is not copied.
It is written as ${MCP_NOTION_TOKEN}; Instabox adds the real value to requests to mcp.notion.com only.
  Store it once:  printf %s "$TOKEN" | npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set MCP_NOTION_TOKEN --host mcp.notion.com
Added notion to ~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json. Every cloud subagent you start from now on gets it.
```

Run the stored-once command with the real token in `$TOKEN`. It must be an Instabox secret created with your `instabox login` session. Creating a secret with the Instabox API key from your cloudy-cloud config fails with `missing_scope: workspace:admin`. If you have not signed in, run `npx --yes instabox@latest login` first.

The list is read each time a subagent starts, so you do not need to restart `cloudy-cloud`. Subagents that are already running keep the servers they started with.

### Where the server is found

It searches your Claude Code settings in this order and uses the first match: the local scope (the entry for the current folder in `~/.claude.json`), the project scope (`.mcp.json` in the repo root), then the user scope (`mcpServers` in `~/.claude.json`). The first output line says which one it used. If the name is not found, it prints `No MCP server named NAME in your Claude Code config. See: claude mcp list` and exits with status 1.

If the name is already in the list, the command prints `Replacing the existing NAME entry.` and overwrites it.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `cloudy-cloud mcp add NAME` | Copies one server from Claude Code's settings to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json`. A token is replaced by a reference and the command to store it is printed. |
| `cloudy-cloud mcp add NAME --allow-literal` | The consent path. See Putting the real token on the machine. |
| `cloudy-cloud mcp ls` | Lists the servers subagents get, one per line: name, type, target (the host, or the `npx` or `uvx` package) and the secrets it needs. With none, it prints `No MCP servers are shared with cloud subagents. Add one with: cloudy-cloud mcp add <name>`. |
| `cloudy-cloud mcp rm NAME` | Removes one server from the list. It does not delete the Instabox secret; use `npx --yes instabox@latest secrets rm MCP_NAME_TOKEN` for that. |

Any other `cloudy-cloud mcp` command, such as `cloudy-cloud mcp list`, goes to Claude Code's own `claude mcp`.

## What can be copied

A cloud machine cannot reach your computer, so only two kinds of server work:

- **Remote servers** of type `http` or `sse` with an `https` URL on a public host. Headers are allowed.
- **`npx` and `uvx` servers** (stdio). The command must be exactly `npx` or `uvx`, because those are installed on the machine.

Everything else is refused with a reason on the line `Not added: REASON`, and `mcp add` exits with status 1:

| Reason you may see | Why |
|---|---|
| `the command is X; only npx and uvx servers can run on a cloud machine` | A local program or script is not on the machine. |
| `arg X is a local path, which does not exist on the machine` | An argument starts with `/`, contains `~` or has a `..` part. |
| `url points at localhost, which does not exist on the machine` | The host is `localhost`, `*.local`, `0.0.0.0`, `::1`, or a `127.*`, `10.*`, `192.168.*` or `172.16-31.*` address. |
| `url must be https` | Plain `http` URLs are not copied. |
| `uses OAuth sign-in, which a headless subagent cannot complete` | A subagent cannot open a browser to sign in. |
| `uses headersHelper, a local script the machine does not have` | The script would not exist on the machine. |
| `type X is not supported on a cloud machine` | Only `http`, `sse` and stdio are accepted. |
| `url carries a secret value; send it in a header instead, ...` and `an argument carries a secret value; pass it in env instead, ...` | A key in a URL or an argument would sit on the machine as plain text. Instabox replaces tokens only in request headers. |
| `references ${X}; cloud machines only expand MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN secrets` | Other `${...}` variables are not available on the machine. |

The same checks run again every time a subagent starts, on whatever is in `mcp.json`.

> Warning: These are limits of the current version: no OAuth servers, no servers that run from a local path or listen on localhost, no secrets in URLs or arguments, and no `sse` servers for the `pi` profiles (pi has no SSE transport).

## Tokens and secrets

The token is never written to `mcp.json`. `mcp add` replaces each secret value in `env` or `headers` with `${MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN}`. `NAME` is the server name in capitals with `-` changed to `_`, so `notion` becomes `MCP_NOTION_TOKEN`. A second secret on the same server is `MCP_<NAME>_2_TOKEN`, and so on. A header is treated as secret when it is `Authorization`, its value starts with `Bearer`, its name ends in `KEY`, `TOKEN`, `SECRET` or `PASSWORD`, or the value looks like a known key format. The same name rule applies to `env` values.

You store the real value once in Instabox with the command `mcp add` prints:

```
printf %s "$TOKEN" | npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set MCP_NOTION_TOKEN --host mcp.notion.com
```

- For a remote server, `--host` is the URL's host.
- For an `npx` or `uvx` server, `mcp add` asks `Which HTTPS hosts does this server send the token to? (comma-separated, exact hostnames, required)`. It does not accept an empty answer. It also needs a terminal for that question. Without one it prints `Not added: a secret without a host list would be sent to any host the subagent reaches.`
- Never create the secret without `--host`. Instabox would then add the value to a request to any host, so a prompt injection could send it to a server the attacker controls.
- Instabox replaces the placeholder only in HTTPS request headers sent to the listed hosts. Both `Authorization: Bearer ...` and a custom header name were checked this way, from `curl` and from Node `fetch`. To other hosts the machine's placeholder stays a placeholder.

When a subagent starts, all the secret names it needs are attached to its machine together with `GH_TOKEN`. If one does not exist, the start fails with a message such as:

```
The Instabox secret MCP_NOTION_TOKEN could not be attached. Create it with: printf %s "$TOKEN" | npx --yes instabox@latest secrets set MCP_NOTION_TOKEN --host <host>
```

If the Instabox error does not name the secret, the message is the usual `GH_TOKEN` one, followed by `Secrets tried: GH_TOKEN, MCP_NOTION_TOKEN`.

Two server names that map to the same secret name (`my-srv` and `my_srv`) cannot both be added. `mcp add` prints `Not added: OTHER already uses MCP_MY_SRV_TOKEN. Rename one of the two servers in Claude Code first.`

> Note: A subagent can still *use* the token against the listed hosts, the way it can use `GH_TOKEN` against GitHub. It cannot read the real value.

### Putting the real token on the machine

Some servers cannot work with a placeholder, for example one that does not send the token in a header. For those, `cloudy-cloud mcp add NAME --allow-literal` keeps the real value in `mcp.json` and copies it to the machine of each subagent you start. A coordinator's own session gets it, but the workers a coordinator starts do not: consent is not passed down, so those workers skip the server. It only applies to values in `env` and `headers`. It is off unless you pass the flag.

> Warning: With `--allow-literal`, the real token sits on the machine in a file with mode 600. Cloud machines run Claude with permission checks off, so a prompt injection in a web page or file could make the agent send that token anywhere. Use a token you can revoke and that has the least access it needs.

The command prints this warning, then asks `Copy the real NAME token onto cloud machines? [y/N]`. Anything other than `y` or `yes` cancels it with `Not added. Run without --allow-literal to keep the token in Instabox.` It also needs a terminal, so you can confirm. Without one it prints `Not added: --allow-literal needs a terminal so you can confirm.` No Instabox secret is created for a server added this way. The entry in `mcp.json` gets `"cloudyCloudAllowLiteral": true`, which is removed before the file is sent to the machine. Remove the server with `cloudy-cloud mcp rm NAME`.

## Files and what the machine gets

- `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json` on your computer, in Claude Code's own format: `{"mcpServers": {...}}`. `mcp add` writes it with mode 600 in a folder with mode 700. Set `CLOUDY_CLOUD_MCP` to use another path. If the file does not exist, the feature is off and nothing changes. If it is not valid JSON, `cloud_agent` fails with `Could not read FILE: ...` and the parse error.
- On each cloud machine, the checked servers are written to `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/mcp.json` (mode 600), and Claude is started with `--mcp-config` for that file and `--strict-mcp-config`. This happens only for Claude subagents and only when at least one server passed the checks.
- On a `pi` or `omp` worker the file goes to `~/pi-agent/mcp.json` or `~/omp-agent/mcp.json` instead (mode 600, folder mode 700). The servers and the `MCP_<NAME>_TOKEN` Instabox secrets are the same. `pi` has no SSE transport, so `sse` servers are skipped for `pi` workers and the reply says `MCP servers skipped: NAME (pi does not support the SSE transport)`. `omp` accepts `sse`. `omp` is also set to ignore MCP servers from other tools and from the repo's own config, so only these servers load.
- Because of `--strict-mcp-config`, a repo's own `.mcp.json` is not loaded on the machine once you have a server in the list. Without the list, nothing changes from before.
- Coordinators get the same list. The list holds references, not secret values, so it adds no secret to a coordinator machine.

## See which servers a subagent had

- **The reply footer** ends with a line such as `MCP servers: notion, context7 (failed: linear)`. It lists the servers that connected and, in brackets, the ones that did not. If none connected it says `MCP servers: none connected`.
- If you allowed a real token, another line says `MCP servers with a real token on the machine (you allowed it): NAME`.
- Entries that did not pass the checks appear as `MCP servers skipped: NAME (REASON)`.
- For a `pi` or `omp` worker the line is `MCP servers: a, b`, the names of the servers that were delivered to the machine. Unlike Claude's start-up report, it does not confirm that a server connected.
- **`cloud_agent_list`** shows a line `mcp notion, context7` under each subagent that has servers.
- **The dashboard** shows an MCP row in the agent's details with the server names. It never shows entries or tokens.

The footer lines appear only when the list has servers or skipped entries.


---

Source: https://cloudycloud.tech/docs/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting, security and FAQ

> Fix common errors, see which credentials reach the cloud, and read answers to common questions.

Find the message you see, what causes it, and the command that fixes it. The security and FAQ sections follow.

## Troubleshooting

### "cloudy-cloud is not set up yet"

A key is missing from `~/.config/cloudy-cloud/env`. In a terminal, `cloudy-cloud` asks `Run setup now? [Y/n]`. Without a terminal it exits with status 1. Run setup yourself:

```
cloudy-cloud setup
```

If you changed a key but the session still uses the old one, restart `cloudy-cloud`. It reads keys once, at start.

### The installer rejects a key

- `Got 103 of 108 characters, so it looks cut off`: the Claude token was cut short when pasted. Press Enter at the Claude step so the installer gets the token itself, or copy the whole token again.
